attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: Keeps the causal core and the three named replacements. It shortens the 'at the price point they were used to' rate-limit element, but the contract restores it.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary. It asks for evidence that unsustainable allowances drove growth and forced the change, and it does not require the product to become unusable.

evidence.note: Cursor's own disclosure confirms the switch from request-based pricing to a $20 usage credit, and admits it explained this poorly. That backs the replacement part only. It says nothing on margins or what drove growth.
The June 30 revision let existing users keep the 500-request plan. That weakens 'had to replace' for everyone, but we don't know if the option still existed on July 21.
Independent report that some users ran out of usage fast and were billed unexpectedly. It supports reduced access for some users, but not how widespread this was or what caused growth.

reviews.rationale: The evidence shows Cursor replaced request-based pricing with usage credits, explained it poorly, and left some users with less access. The core claim is causal: that growth came from unsustainable allowances. Nothing in the packet covers growth drivers, serving costs or margins, and the opt-out option cuts against a forced replacement. The packet does not settle the causal claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the $500M milestone, the 'can no longer afford' claim and the industry-wide inference. It drops the 'growth story was a lie' framing, which the contract reads as being about sustainability. That is reasonable.

contract.note: Reading 'cannot afford' as economically unsustainable rather than insolvent is fair and ordinary. Treating the industry-wide part as a suggestion matches his word 'suggesting'. The ARR-versus-annualized distinction is fairly flagged.

evidence.note: TechCrunch cites unnamed sources saying Cursor passed $500M ARR. The method is not given, and ARR is not matched to the contract's annualized-revenue metric, so this is only corroboration.
Cursor's disclosure says per-request costs vary widely, and that most users' costs have stayed fairly constant. That limits any inference of unaffordability. It gives no margins.

reviews.rationale: The revenue milestone is reported, but only as ARR from unnamed sources, and that metric is not matched to the contract's. The central element, that the former offering could not be afforded, needs serving-cost and margin data the packet lacks. Cursor's note about most users cuts against the claim without settling it. Nothing tests the claim about all coding startups.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words. The five companies are the ones named in his own section heading.

semantics.note: The causal claim and the 'not going to die' qualifier are kept. Treating 'will be' as describing a present structural dependence fits the context.

contract.note: Reading 'largely dictate' as 'a leading determinant' is a fair plain reading of firm language. Requiring causal attribution rather than index weight alone is reasonable.

evidence.note: The ECB (May 2025) calls US equity concentration a vulnerability, citing the DeepSeek sell-off. That supports a general concentration risk, but it does not measure how much the five buyers' NVIDIA spending drives market stability.
The Fed's survey names trade, policy and fiscal risks, among others. That suggests several drivers but does not quantify or rule out a dependence on NVIDIA spending.

reviews.rationale: The packet has central-bank material on market concentration and on competing risks. It has no causal breakdown linking broad US market instability to the named buyers' NVIDIA purchases, and the contract's support and contradiction conditions both require one. The evidence available does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words. He draws the figures from press reporting and adopts them as his own conclusion.

semantics.note: The core share, near-cost pricing, $3B remainder and 3.75% figures are kept. It leaves out the 16.25% figure and the claim that OpenAI revenue costs Microsoft more than it earns, but the contract covers both.

contract.note: The contract keeps the annualized $13B basis and the FY2025 $80B plan, which match the speaker's own context. It treats 'real' revenue as his own subtraction, which is fair.

evidence.note: Microsoft's earnings call confirms an AI run rate of more than $13B, the denominator. It gives no OpenAI split, so the 76.9% share and the near-cost claim are unverified.
CNBC confirms Microsoft planned to spend $80B on AI data centers in FY2025 (planned, not realized). This checks the denominator only.

reviews.rationale: Both denominators are confirmed: the $13B AI run rate and the $80B FY2025 plan. The arithmetic is correct for those inputs. The decisive inputs are unsupported: the $10B OpenAI share, near-cost pricing, and the claim that OpenAI revenue costs more than it earns. The cited reporting could not be read. Correct arithmetic does not verify the financial claims.
